content.title: About
content.content: Millet, whole grain is the edible seed of the millet plant (Panicum miliaceum) cultivated in warm regions worldwide. It has a mild nutty flavor, a slightly sweet aroma, and a soft, gently crunchy texture when cooked. Millet is used as a grain, flour, flakes, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Millet is one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown by humans for over 7,000 years.
Unlike most cereals, millet is naturally gluten‑free, making it suitable for gluten‑free diets.
Millet is drought‑tolerant and can thrive in poor soils, which is why it is important in arid regions.
In several cultures millet is featured in traditional ceremonial dishes and festivals.
Millet is rich in antioxidants, including phenolic compounds that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain millet provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in millet aids normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron contributes to normal hemoglobin levels and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Millet raises blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people managing diabetes or weight.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B3, and B6 vitamins in millet support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to millet.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; soaking or sprouting millet can mitigate this.

items.title: Pesticide residue
items.content: When buying raw millet, choose products from reputable sources to minimize pesticide exposure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Millet can be boiled as a porridge, added to salads, soups, casseroles, or used to make bread and pancakes. Before cooking, rinse and soak the grains for 4–6 hours to shorten cooking time and improve digestibility. Toasting millet in a dry pan brings out a pleasant nutty flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole‑grain millet in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation. Discard millet that smells stale, rancid, or off.
